agents.name: Pembrolizumab
agents.explanation: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.
agents.watch: Report new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.

day_groups.title: Infusion and assessment
day_groups.body: The team reviews blood results, symptoms and medicines. Tell the nurse immediately about itching, flushing, tight chest, dizziness or suddenly feeling unwell.
day_groups.action: Confirm the next tests, treatment visit and contact plan.

day_groups.title: Between infusions
day_groups.body: Immune effects may start at any time. A long interval between treatment visits is not a break from symptom reporting.
day_groups.action: Keep thyroid tests every 3–6 weeks, including separate appointments if required.

support.title: Routine medicines
support.text: Routine premedication is not usually required. Pembrolizumab has minimal emetogenic potential; the team individualises anti-sickness treatment if needed.

support.title: Steroids and hormone replacement
support.text: If immune effects develop, the team may prescribe steroids or hormones. Follow the exact plan; do not stop steroids abruptly or restart pembrolizumab yourself. If treatment is paused because of an immune side effect, your team checks recovery and any steroid or hormone plan before deciding whether it can restart. Do not change steroids or restart treatment yourself.

support.title: Medicines and pregnancy
support.text: Bring prescription, non-prescription and herbal medicines. Discuss pregnancy prevention; effective contraception is required during pembrolizumab and for at least four months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment.

scope_note: This guide covers first-line metastatic MSI-H/dMMR colorectal cancer. The shared NCCP regimen has other cancer indications, but their tests, treatment aims and durations are not this guide.

evidence.title: Evidence in MSI-H/dMMR colorectal cancer
evidence.intro: KEYNOTE-177 compared pembrolizumab 200 mg every three weeks with chemotherapy in previously untreated MSI-H/dMMR metastatic colorectal cancer.
evidence.population: Previously untreated MSI-H/dMMR metastatic colorectal cancer; trial participants had ECOG 0–1.
evidence.interpretation: The trial showed a longer time before cancer worsened with pembrolizumab. This is a group result, not a guarantee for one person; ask your team about benefits, risks and alternatives in your situation.
evidence.limitations: This evidence is specific to the tumour feature and treatment setting. The 400 mg six-week regimen uses exposure bridging; it should not be described as a separate colorectal randomised trial.

chapters.title: Your colorectal cancer and treatment aim
chapters.intro: The tumour test and treatment setting matter.

items.title: MSI-H and dMMR
items.text: These tests identify a problem with the cancer’s DNA-repair system. They help identify colorectal cancers more likely to benefit from this immunotherapy. Ask whether genetics assessment is relevant to you.

items.title: First-line metastatic treatment
items.text: Pembrolizumab aims to control bowel cancer that has spread and has a particular DNA-repair feature, called MSI-H or dMMR. Your team discusses likely benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for you. First-line means the first systemic treatment for the metastatic setting.

items.title: Your choices
items.text: Ask about other treatments, clinical trials and symptom-focused care, how benefit will be assessed and what matters to your quality of life.

chapters.title: How pembrolizumab works
chapters.intro: It releases a brake on immune cells.

items.title: PD-1 blockade
items.text: Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.

items.title: Healthy tissues can be affected
items.text: The same immune activation can inflame the bowel, lungs, liver, kidneys, skin, hormone glands, heart, nerves or muscles. Some effects require hospital care, steroids or lasting hormone replacement.

items.title: A pause is a safety decision
items.text: Doses may be delayed or treatment stopped for immune effects. The standard approach is to hold or stop treatment, not simply to give a smaller dose. Feeling better or having normal tests does not by itself mean that pembrolizumab can restart. Your team reviews what happened, recovery and the steroid or hormone plan. Some reactions mean that treatment must remain stopped, even if the symptoms have settled. Follow the prescribed plan and never restart treatment or change steroids yourself. Restart depends on the original reaction, recovery and any steroid or hormone plan. Some reactions mean treatment must remain stopped even after symptoms settle.

chapters.title: Your treatment course
chapters.intro: Visit frequency and total course length are separate decisions.

items.title: Infusions
items.text: Pembrolizumab 200 mg is given over about 30 minutes on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The visit takes longer for assessment and preparation.

items.title: Course reviews
items.text: Continue while treatment helps and side effects remain acceptable. At 24 months, the team may consider stopping if there is a sustained response without progression; this is an individual review, not an automatic fixed final cycle.

items.title: Evidence for the schedule
items.text: KEYNOTE-177 tested 200 mg every three weeks. The 400 mg six-week schedule is supported by exposure bridging and product authorisation; it was not a separate randomised colorectal comparison.

chapters.title: Tests and follow-up
chapters.intro: Blood tests can identify a problem before symptoms appear.

items.title: Before starting
items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver function, glucose and thyroid function at baseline. Blood count, kidney/liver and glucose before each 3-weekly cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks regardless of infusion interval; cortisol if indicated. Scans and markers follow the consultant plan.

items.title: Scans and tumour markers
items.text: The consultant sets the disease-assessment plan. This regimen does not prescribe a universal CT or CEA interval. A scan schedule from a research study is not automatically your schedule.

items.title: During a hold and after stopping
items.text: Keep follow-up appointments and the agreed steroid or hormone plan. Continue reporting symptoms after the last dose; another clinician needs to know you have received immunotherapy.

items.title: Bowel changes
items.text: Report new or persistent diarrhoea, blood in stools or abdominal pain promptly. Do not treat ongoing diarrhoea as a minor stomach upset or rely on self-treatment without advice.

items.title: Energy and hormones
items.text: New marked fatigue, headache, dizziness, feeling unusually cold, unusual thirst or passing more urine may need hormone and glucose tests.

items.title: Medicines, pregnancy and feeding
items.text: Bring prescription, non-prescription and herbal medicines. Discuss pregnancy prevention; effective contraception is required during pembrolizumab and for at least four months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Do not wait for the next infusion.

items.title: Warning symptoms
items.text: Contact oncology immediately for new breathlessness, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin or eyes, much less urine, spreading or blistering rash, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse or seizure needs emergency care. Effects can begin after treatment ends.

items.title: During the infusion
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately about itching, flushing, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell.

items.title: Carry the alert card
items.text: Show your treatment card to any healthcare team, even after immunotherapy ends. Keep your actual daytime and out-of-hours oncology numbers accessible.

items.title: When heart, muscle and nerve symptoms overlap
items.text: Heart, muscle and nerve problems can occur together. New muscle pain or weakness with changed vision, unusual tiredness, breathlessness, chest pain or an irregular heartbeat needs immediate medical advice. Do not wait for several symptoms to appear together. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or rapidly worsening weakness needs emergency care.
